Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 62
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Potter
  trauma_type: Unexpected or traumatic death of a loved one
  pcl5: 60

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Positive Feelings: push away positive emotions because they feel unsafe, Avoid Grief Reminders: Anything that reminds me of someone I have lost, Avoid Future Plans: Making any plans for the future

Vignette:
Harold Beaumont is a 62-year-old potter who lives with his wife on a small rural property in western Oregon, where he has worked clay for nearly three decades. He came to his first appointment quietly, carrying the particular stillness of a man who had learned to hold himself very carefully, as though sudden movement might dislodge something he could not afford to lose.

Fourteen months ago, Harold's son Daniel, thirty-one years old and in apparent good health, collapsed without warning at a weekend soccer game and was pronounced dead at the scene from an undetected cardiac arrhythmia. Harold had been there. He had been standing along the sideline watching Daniel play, the same way he had watched him play since Daniel was seven years old, when his son simply dropped mid-stride and did not get up. There was no illness, no premonition, no period of anticipatory grief to soften what happened. One moment Harold was watching his son run; the next, he was on his knees beside him on the grass, calling his name. The paramedics worked for a long time. Harold watched all of it. He has not spoken about the details of those minutes to anyone, including his wife.

In the weeks that followed, Harold continued to go to his studio each day, but something had changed in the nature of that time. The studio had always been a place of absorption and quiet pleasure — the feel of wet clay, the smell of the kiln, the particular satisfaction of a form coming right. Those sensations began to feel dangerous to him. When he noticed himself becoming absorbed in the work, or felt something close to contentment settle over him, he would find reasons to stop. He might wash his hands and go inside, or find some administrative task that needed doing. He had come to believe that allowing himself to feel good was a form of betrayal — that pleasure had no legitimate place in a life from which Daniel had been removed. What frightened him most was not the grief itself but the moments when the grief briefly lifted, because those moments felt like a forgetting, and forgetting felt like a second loss he could not survive.

He began to avoid anything that carried Daniel's presence. A particular coffee mug Daniel had given him as a gift disappeared into a cabinet. Harold stopped listening to the radio station they had both liked. He declined invitations to the soccer club's end-of-season gathering, where Daniel's name was to be mentioned. His wife, Renata, noticed that he would leave a room when photographs came up on the television screensaver. She has said very little about this, uncertain how to reach him, and Harold is aware that something has grown between them that he does not know how to name.

He stopped making plans. This began almost immediately after Daniel's death and has hardened over the months into something close to a rule. He and Renata had spoken vaguely about a trip to Portugal the following spring. He cannot discuss it. When a gallery owner he has worked with for years asked him about a commission for the following autumn, Harold said he would think about it and has not returned the call. He has come to feel that planning implies a future, and that assuming any future for himself is a presumption he is no longer entitled to make. His order book, once scheduled six months out, is now empty beyond the next few weeks.

The occupational consequences have become impossible to ignore. Three long-standing gallery relationships have quietly lapsed. His income has dropped significantly, and Renata, who has been patient and careful with him, recently said in a measured way that she was worried about them practically as well as personally. It was that conversation, Harold said, that finally brought him in. He had not wanted to come. He is not certain he believes that talking will help. What he is most afraid of, he said at the end of the first session, is that if he allows himself to grieve fully and openly, he will find that there is nothing left of him on the other side of it. What he is hoping for, though he offered this almost inaudibly, is that he might one day be able to sit in his studio and feel the clay in his hands without it feeling like something he has stolen.
